proofs.proof_tex:
Let \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  By lower triangularity, every power \(A^r\) is lower triangular and has diagonal \((A^r)_{ii}=A_{ii}^r\).  The transition equation in \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) therefore gives, coordinate by coordinate,
\[
B_{ii}=(A^m)_{ii}=A_{ii}^m.
\]
The assumption \(\texttt{ass:odd-factor}\) makes \(x\mapsto x^m\) injective on \(\mathbb R\).  Hence every compatible pair has the same diagonal,
\[
A_{ii}=B_{ii}^{1/m},
\]
where the right-hand side denotes the unique real \(m\)-th root.

We next determine the lower off-diagonal entries by induction on the endpoint gap \(g=i-j\).  Set every upper-triangular entry and every graph-forbidden lower-triangular entry to zero, as required respectively by \(\texttt{ass:lower-triangular}\) and \(\texttt{ass:graph-support}\).  Suppose that all allowed entries with endpoint gap smaller than \(g\) have already been determined, and let \(j\to i\) be an allowed edge with \(i-j=g\).  The established lemma \(\texttt{lem:path-expansion}\) gives
\[
B_{ij}=(A^m)_{ij}
=A_{ij}C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})+R_{ij,m}(A).
\]
Every off-diagonal factor in every monomial of \(R_{ij,m}(A)\) has endpoint gap strictly smaller than \(g\), so the induction hypothesis and the graph zeros determine this remainder.  By the stated noncollision hypothesis, \((A_{ii},A_{jj})\ne(0,0)\).  The odd part of the established lemma \(\texttt{lem:divided-difference-zero-set}\) therefore yields
\[
C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})>0.
\]
Division is consequently valid and forces
\[
A_{ij}
=\frac{B_{ij}-R_{ij,m}(A)}{C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})}.
\]
Induction over \(g=1,\ldots,d-1\) determines every allowed lower-triangular entry.  In particular, if \((\widetilde A,\widetilde D)\) is a second compatible pair, its diagonal equals that of \(A\); hence it satisfies the same noncollision inequalities, and the same gap induction gives \(\widetilde A=A\).  Thus the transition matrix is unique whenever the fiber is nonempty.

Fix the recovered \(A\).  Since \(D\) is diagonal by the definition of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\), the \((i,i)\) coordinate of the coarse covariance equation is
\[
Q_{ii}
=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\bigl(A^rD(A^r)^\top\bigr)_{ii}
=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\sum_{j=1}^d D_{jj}(A^r)_{ij}^2.
\]
Lower triangularity gives \((A^r)_{ij}=0\) for \(j>i\), and the diagonal identity above gives \((A^r)_{ii}=A_{ii}^r\).  Consequently
\[
Q_{ii}
=D_{ii}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}
+\sum_{j<i}D_{jj}\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(A^r)_{ij}^2.
\]
The coefficient
\[
s_i:=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}
\]
is strictly positive because its \(r=0\) term equals one.  Starting with \(i=1\) and proceeding upward, the preceding display therefore determines
\[
D_{ii}
=\frac{Q_{ii}-\displaystyle\sum_{j<i}D_{jj}
\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}(A^r)_{ij}^2}
{\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_{ii}^{2r}}.
\]
Thus a compatible diagonal innovation covariance is also unique.  We have proved that every nonempty compatible fiber contains at most one pair; nonemptiness then makes it a singleton.

It remains to prove the advertised compatibility test.  Given arbitrary input \((B,Q)\), form the candidate by the diagonal-root, gap, and innovation recursions above.  The diagonal equations of \(A^m=B\) hold by the definition of the real roots, and its allowed lower-triangular equations hold by the gap recursion.  All structural zeros of \(A\) are imposed during construction.  Therefore checking the remaining, non-recursed coordinates of \(A^m=B\), including every graph-forbidden and upper-triangular coordinate, is equivalent to the full transition equation.  Likewise, the diagonal coordinates of
\[
Q=\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top
\]
hold by the innovation recursion, and checking the displayed complete covariance equation is equivalent to checking all of its remaining coordinates as well.  Because the candidate \(A\) is triangular, the stability condition in the compatible-fiber definition is exactly \(\max_i|A_{ii}|<1\).  Because the candidate \(D\) is diagonal, \(D\succ0\) is exactly the coordinatewise condition \(D_{ii}>0\) for all \(i\).  Hence stability, positivity, the remaining transition checks, and the complete covariance check are jointly sufficient for membership in \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  They are necessary by the definition of that fiber.  This proves the claimed if-and-only-if test.

Finally, by \(\texttt{def:transfer-fiber}\), \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\) is the image of the compatible fiber under
\[
(A,D)\longmapsto
\left[z\longmapsto\frac{A_{vu}z}{1-A_{vv}z}\right].
\]
For \(|z|=1\), stability gives \(|A_{vv}z|<1\), so the denominator is nonzero.  The singleton compatible fiber therefore maps to the singleton containing the structural causal transfer \(h_{uv}\).  This proves equality between the causal target and the observed-law recovery map; it does not define the causal target from the coarse law.

For the required exact regular stress test, let \(d=2\), let \(G\) contain the edge \(1\to2\), take \(m=3\), and set
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\[2pt]1/4&1/3\end{pmatrix},
\qquad D=I_2.
\]
Then
\[
B=A^3
=\begin{pmatrix}1/8&0\\[2pt]19/144&1/27\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
Q=\sum_{r=0}^{2}A^r(A^r)^\top
=\begin{pmatrix}21/16&17/96\\[2pt]17/96&6373/5184\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Indeed,
\[
C_3(1/3,1/2)=\frac19+\frac16+\frac14=\frac{19}{36},
\qquad
A_{21}=\frac{19/144}{19/36}=\frac14.
\]
The first innovation recursion gives \(D_{11}=1\).  For the second, the earlier-coordinate contribution is
\[
\left(\frac14\right)^2+\left(\frac5{24}\right)^2=\frac{61}{576},
\]
while
\[
Q_{22}-\frac{61}{576}=\frac{91}{81}
=1+\left(\frac13\right)^2+\left(\frac13\right)^4,
\]
so \(D_{22}=1\).  The recovered transfer is therefore
\[
h_{12}(z)=\frac{z}{4(1-z/3)}.
\]

The noncollision hypothesis is load-bearing.  With the same graph and \(m=3\), fix \(q_1,q_2>0\) and, for every \(|a|<\sqrt{q_2/q_1}\), define
\[
A(a)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ a&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
D(a)=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2-a^2q_1).
\]
These matrices obey the graph restrictions, \(A(a)\) is stable, and \(D(a)\succ0\).  Since \(A(a)^2=0\), direct multiplication gives
\[
A(a)^3=0,
\qquad
\sum_{r=0}^{2}A(a)^rD(a)(A(a)^r)^\top
=\operatorname{diag}(q_1,q_2).
\]
Thus one coarse law has an open interval of compatible parameters and transfers
\[
h_{12}^{(a)}(z)=az.
\]
Here both endpoint persistences of the allowed edge vanish, exactly violating the excluded condition; hence the identification conclusion genuinely fails when that condition is removed.

Fix the effective \(K\)-valued matrices \(B,Q\), the supplied graph \(G\), and the known integer \(m\geq 2\).  For each compatible structural pair \((A,D)\), the causal target is the transfer \(h_{uv}(z)=A_{vu}z/(1-A_{vv}z)\).  By contrast, \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\) is the image of the compatible structural fiber under this transfer map.  Thus the observed coarse law identifies the causal target precisely when this image is a singleton; this relationship will be proved by the certificate rather than imposed as a definition of the causal target.

Put
\[
 \mathcal I_G
 =\{(i,i):i\in V\}\cup
   \{(i,j):j<i\text{ and }j\to i\text{ in }G\}.
\]
For every \((i,j)\in\mathcal I_G\), introduce a real variable \(a_{ij}\), and introduce real variables \(d_1,\ldots,d_d\).  Let \(\widetilde A(a)\) have entry \(a_{ij}\) on \(\mathcal I_G\) and zero elsewhere, and let \(\widetilde D(d)=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_d)\).  The lower-triangular and graph-support restrictions in the definition of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) are therefore imposed by this coordinate parametrization.

Consider the finite system
\[
 \bigl[\widetilde A(a)^m\bigr]_{ij}=B_{ij}
 \quad(i,j\in V),                                                   \tag{1}
\]
\[
 \left[\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}\widetilde A(a)^r\widetilde D(d)
                    \bigl(\widetilde A(a)^r\bigr)^\top\right]_{ij}
 =Q_{ij}
 \quad(i,j\in V),                                                   \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
 -1<a_{ii}<1\quad(i\in V),
 \qquad d_i>0\quad(i\in V).                                        \tag{3}
\]
Every left-hand side in (1)--(2) is a polynomial in finitely many variables with coefficients in \(K\), by the effective-input assumption.  Since \(\widetilde A(a)\) is triangular,
\[
 \det\!\left(\lambda I-\widetilde A(a)\right)
   =\prod_{i=1}^d(\lambda-a_{ii}),
 \qquad
 \rho\!\left(\widetilde A(a)\right)=\max_i|a_{ii}|.
\]
Consequently the first collection of strict inequalities in (3) is equivalent to stability.  Moreover, for every nonzero \(x\in\mathbb R^d\),
\[
 x^\top\widetilde D(d)x=\sum_{i=1}^d d_i x_i^2>0
\]
if and only if every \(d_i>0\).  Hence the second collection in (3) is equivalent to \(\widetilde D(d)\succ0\).  It follows from the definition of the compatible fiber that
\[
 (a,d)\longmapsto\bigl(\widetilde A(a),\widetilde D(d)\bigr)         \tag{4}
\]
is a bijection from the realization of (1)--(3) onto \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\).  In particular, this encoding neither adds boundary points nor replaces strict positivity or strict stability by their closures.

For a triangular matrix, the diagonal part of (1) is
\[
 a_{ii}^{m}=B_{ii},\qquad i\in V.                                  \tag{5}
\]
Because \(K\) is an effective real closed field, its effective arithmetic, order tests, and real-root isolation enumerate the real roots of each equation (5) and decide the stability inequalities in (3).  There is exactly one real root of \(x^m=b\) when \(m\) is odd.  When \(m\) is even, there are no real roots for \(b<0\), one for \(b=0\), and two for \(b>0\).  Thus there are finitely many surviving diagonal branches, and their coordinates are represented exactly in \(K\).  If no branch survives, (4) shows that the compatible fiber is empty.

Fix one surviving branch and process off-diagonal pairs \((v,u)\) in increasing order of \(v-u\), as prescribed by the graph-recursive root map.  The path-expansion lemma gives
\[
 a_{vu}C_m(a_{vv},a_{uu})
   =B_{vu}-R_{vu,m}(\widetilde A(a)).                               \tag{6}
\]
Every off-diagonal coordinate occurring on the right side of (6) has smaller endpoint gap.  The diagonal entries in
\[
 c_{vu}:=C_m(a_{vv},a_{uu})                                        \tag{7}
\]
are fixed on the branch, so \(c_{vu}\in K\).  The divided-difference zero-set lemma, together with the exact sign tests in \(K\), decides whether \(c_{vu}=0\).  In particular, the odd-factor case \(a_{vv}=a_{uu}=0\) and the even-factor case \(a_{vv}=-a_{uu}\) are retained as singular cases rather than divided through.

If \(u\to v\) is graph-allowed and \(c_{vu}\neq0\), equation (6) is equivalent to the unique substitution
\[
 a_{vu}
 =\frac{B_{vu}-R_{vu,m}(\widetilde A(a))}{c_{vu}}.                 \tag{8}
\]
This division is made only after the nonzero test.  Since \(c_{vu}^{-1}\in K\) is fixed on the branch, substituting (8) into later transition equations and into the covariance equations produces polynomials over \(K\) in the residual variables; there is no variable denominator.  If \(c_{vu}=0\), the coordinate is not eliminated and the induced equation
\[
 B_{vu}-R_{vu,m}(\widetilde A(a))=0                                \tag{9}
\]
is retained.  If the edge is forbidden, \(a_{vu}=0\) by the support parametrization and the transition equation (9) is again retained, irrespective of the value of \(c_{vu}\).

Induction over the endpoint gap proves exactness of the recursion.  At a nonsingular allowed coordinate, every solution of the pre-substitution system must have the value (8), while every solution of the substituted system lifts uniquely through (8).  At a singular or forbidden coordinate, no residual variable or compatibility equation is discarded.  The induction is applicable because the path-expansion lemma places only smaller-gap off-diagonal coordinates in the remainder.  After the finitely many pairs have been processed, every transition equation not already used for an exact substitution, every covariance equation in (2), and every strict inequality in (3) remains imposed after the accumulated substitutions.  Therefore, if \(\mathfrak R_b\) denotes the residual semialgebraic realization on diagonal branch \(b\) and \(\operatorname{Rec}_b\) denotes reconstruction by the substitutions, then
\[
 \mathcal S(B,Q;G)
   =\bigcup_b \operatorname{Rec}_b(\mathfrak R_b).                 \tag{10}
\]
This is literal set equality, not equality after topological or algebraic closure.

Each \(\mathfrak R_b\) is a finite Boolean combination of polynomial equalities and strict polynomial inequalities over \(K\).  There are finitely many branches and finitely many variables.  The effective CAD decision-and-sampling lemma therefore implies that CAD terminates on every branch, decides whether \(\mathfrak R_b\) is empty, and returns an exact represented sample point whenever it is nonempty.  By (10), all branch systems are empty if and only if \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)=\varnothing\).  This proves termination, soundness, and completeness of the incompatibility output.

It remains to classify the transfer fiber.  Suppose that the compatible fiber is nonempty, take two compatible points, and write
\[
 p=A_{vu},\quad q=A_{vv},\qquad
 p'=A'_{vu},\quad q'=A'_{vv}.
\]
Stability gives \(|q|<1\) and \(|q'|<1\).  Hence, for every \(z\in\mathbb T\),
\[
 |qz|<1,\qquad |q'z|<1,
\]
so neither \(1-qz\) nor \(1-q'z\) vanishes.  Since also \(z\neq0\) on \(\mathbb T\), cross multiplication and cancellation of \(z\) are valid.  The two transfers agree on \(\mathbb T\) if and only if
\[
 p(1-q'z)=p'(1-qz)\quad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb T.             \tag{11}
\]
The difference between the sides of (11) is
\[
 (p-p')+(p'q-pq')z.                                                 \tag{12}
\]
Evaluating (12) at \(z=1\) and \(z=-1\) shows that it vanishes on \(\mathbb T\) if and only if both coefficients vanish.  Thus
\[
 h_{p,q}=h_{p',q'}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 p=p'\ \text{ and }\ pq'=p'q,                                    \tag{13}
\]
and, since all four coefficients are real,
\[
 h_{p,q}\neq h_{p',q'}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \Delta(p,q,p',q')
 :=(p-p')^2+(pq'-p'q)^2>0.                                        \tag{14}
\]
Equation (13) correctly treats all pairs \((0,q)\) as representing the same zero transfer; equality of coefficient pairs is neither required nor used.

For every ordered pair of diagonal branches, take two copies of their complete residual systems and append the strict polynomial inequality (14), expressed after reconstruction.  The resulting finite union of two-copy systems is feasible if and only if two points of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) have unequal transfers, by (10) and (14).  The CAD lemma decides this feasibility and, when it holds, supplies exact residual sample points.  Reconstruction yields attained pairs
\[
 (A,D),(A',D')\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)
\]
satisfying
\[
 (A_{vu}-A'_{vu})^2
 +(A_{vu}A'_{vv}-A'_{vu}A_{vv})^2>0.
\]
Their strict stability and innovation-positivity inequalities are inherited from their one-copy branch systems.  This proves soundness of the ambiguity output, while the feasibility equivalence proves its completeness.

If every two-copy system is infeasible, (14) says that every two compatible points yield the same transfer.  An exact sample from any nonempty one-copy branch supplies \((p,q)\) and hence the common exact rational function
\[
 z\longmapsto\frac{pz}{1-qz}.
\]
Conversely, if \(\mathcal H_{uv}(B,Q;G)\) is a singleton, no two-copy system can satisfy (14), and the certificate returns this common function.  Thus the singleton output is equivalent to point identification of the causal transfer, and the three advertised outputs are exhaustive.

The same equivalences cover every stated exceptional case.  Zero diagonal roots remain among the solutions of (5) and enter a residual singular system whenever their divided difference vanishes.  A graph-forbidden queried edge, or an allowed queried edge forced to zero by compatibility, is treated correctly by (13).  The CAD lemma applies directly to open and positive-dimensional fibers with the strict inequalities (3).  Branch duplication or merger cannot change the result because (10) is a union and the two-copy test ranges over every ordered branch pair.  No rank, overlap, conditioning, or limiting condition is invoked, and the sole divisions in the recursion occur under the explicit nonvanishing condition in (8).

For the first required exact stress test, take \(d=2\), \(m=3\), let \(G\) contain \(1\to2\), and set \(B=0\) and \(Q=I_2\).  Define
\[
 A_{\pm}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ \pm\tfrac12&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 D_{\pm}=\operatorname{diag}\!\left(1,\tfrac34\right).
\]
Then \(A_{\pm}^2=0\), and hence
\[
 A_{\pm}^3=0=B,
 \qquad
 \sum_{r=0}^{2}A_{\pm}^rD_{\pm}(A_{\pm}^r)^\top
 =D_{\pm}+A_{\pm}D_{\pm}A_{\pm}^\top
 =\operatorname{diag}\!\left(1,\tfrac34\right)
  +\operatorname{diag}\!\left(0,\tfrac14\right)
 =I_2.
\]
Both points satisfy the strict inequalities \(\rho(A_{\pm})=0<1\) and \(D_{\pm}\succ0\), while their transfers are \(z/2\) and \(-z/2\).  They are attained, strictly stable, strictly innovation-positive, transfer-distinct witnesses, so the exact two-copy test cannot return either a singleton or a boundary-only artifact.

For the second stress test, let \(d=2\), \(m=2\), and let \((A,D)\) be any compatible point with \(A_{21}\neq0\).  The lower-triangular and graph-support zeros are preserved by \(A\mapsto-A\), as are stability and positivity of \(D\), while
\[
 (-A)^2=A^2,
 \qquad
 D+(-A)D(-A)^\top=D+ADA^\top.
\]
Thus \((-A,D)\) is a second compatible point for the same \((B,Q)\).  With \(p=A_{21}\), \(q=A_{22}\), \(p'=-p\), and \(q'=-q\),
\[
 \Delta(p,q,-p,-q)
 =(2p)^2+\{p(-q)-(-p)q\}^2
 =4p^2>0.
\]
Consequently every nonzero-edge two-variable \(m=2\) compatible case retains its global sign pair, as required.

Put
\[
 \mathfrak P_{\partial}
 =\mathcal M_{\mathrm{reg}}^{\partial}
 (d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max},\kappa)
\]
and let \(\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}\) denote the target-corridor class in
\(\mathrm{def{:}corridor\mbox{-}derivative\mbox{-}separated\mbox{-}class}\),
with the same displayed arguments.  By
\(\mathrm{def{:}regular\mbox{-}class}\) and
\(\mathrm{def{:}derivative\mbox{-}separated\mbox{-}regular\mbox{-}class}\),
each \(P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}\) belongs to the compact class, has odd
\(m\), and satisfies
\[
 m|A_{ii}|^{m-1}\geq\kappa\quad(i\in V),
 \qquad
 |C_m(A_{ii},A_{jj})|\geq\kappa\quad(j\to i\in E).
 \tag{1}
\]
The inclusions \(V_{uv}^{G}\subseteq V\) and
\(E_{uv}^{G}\subseteq E\), which follow directly from
\(\mathrm{def{:}target\mbox{-}corridor}\), show by restricting the two
minima in \((1)\) that
\[
 \mathfrak P_{\partial}\subseteq\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}.
 \tag{2}
\]
Moreover, the hypotheses that the labels are topologically ordered, that
\(u\to v\in G\), and that
\(\kappa\leq m(1-\gamma)^{m-1}\), together with
\(\mathrm{lem{:}derivative\mbox{-}separated\mbox{-}class\mbox{-}nonempty}\),
give
\[
 \mathfrak P_{\partial}\neq\varnothing.
 \tag{3}
\]
Thus the class over which the asserted uniform limit is taken is
nonempty.

We next establish that the full and corridor estimators agree with
probability tending to one uniformly on \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\).  The
needed neighborhood statement can be obtained directly from the compact
class conditions.  Indeed, a lower-triangular matrix in that class obeys,
for constants \(C_0<\infty\) and \(r_0\in(0,1)\) depending only on
\(d,\gamma,L\),
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}\|A^r\|
 \leq C_0r_0^r,
 \qquad r\geq0.
 \tag{4}
\]
To verify \((4)\), expand an entry of \(A^r\) over nondecreasing index
walks.  Such a walk has at most \(d-1\) strict increases.  Its terms with
\(q\) strict increases are bounded by
\(L^q(1-\gamma)^{r-q}\), and their number is bounded by a constant times
\((r+1)^q\).  Summing over \(0\leq q\leq d-1\) and absorbing the resulting
fixed-degree polynomial into \(r_0^r/(1-\gamma)^r\), for any fixed
\(r_0\in(1-\gamma,1)\), proves \((4)\).

Stationarity and the innovation bounds in
\(\mathrm{def{:}compact\mbox{-}class}\) now give
\[
 M_0=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}A^rD(A^r)^\top,
 \qquad
 d_{\min}I_d\preceq M_0\preceq C_1I_d,
 \tag{5}
\]
where \(C_1<\infty\) is uniform on \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\).  Since
\(B=A^m\), the coarse autocovariances satisfy
\[
 \mathbb E_P[Y_{s+k}Y_s^\top]=B^kM_0\quad(k\geq0),
 \qquad
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}
 \|B^kM_0\|\leq C_2r_0^{mk}.
 \tag{6}
\]
For four coordinates of a centered jointly Gaussian vector,
differentiating its moment-generating function four times at zero gives
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}(U_1U_2,U_3U_4)
 =\operatorname{Cov}(U_1,U_3)\operatorname{Cov}(U_2,U_4)
  +\operatorname{Cov}(U_1,U_4)\operatorname{Cov}(U_2,U_3).
 \tag{7}
\]
Applying \((7)\) to the entries of
\(Y_sY_s^\top\) and \(Y_sY_{s-1}^\top\), and then using \((6)\), yields
a constant \(C_3<\infty\) such that every scalar coordinate \(Z_s\) of
these two product arrays satisfies
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}
 \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}
 \bigl|\operatorname{Cov}_P(Z_0,Z_k)\bigr|\leq C_3.
 \tag{8}
\]
Consequently, by the definitions in
\(\mathrm{def{:}empirical\mbox{-}moments}\),
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}
 \mathbb E_P\!\left[
  \|\widehat M_0-M_0\|^2+\|\widehat M_1-M_1\|^2
 \right]
 \leq \frac{C_4}{n}.
 \tag{9}
\]
Here and below any fixed matrix norm may be used, since \(d\) is fixed.
The lower eigenvalue bound in \((5)\), the inverse identity
\(U^{-1}-V^{-1}=U^{-1}(V-U)V^{-1}\), and
\(B=M_1M_0^{-1}\) therefore imply
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}P(\widehat M_0\not\succ0)
 \longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}
 P\!\left(\|\widehat B-B\|>\delta\right)\longrightarrow0
 \quad\text{for every }\delta>0.
 \tag{10}
\]

At a population value from \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\), the inverse
diagonal map \(b\mapsto b^{1/m}\) is differentiable at
\(b=A_{ii}^m\), with derivative
\[
 \frac{1}{mA_{ii}^{m-1}},
 \tag{11}
\]
whose absolute value is at most \(\kappa^{-1}\) by \((1)\).  Every
off-diagonal division in the full graph recursion has denominator of
absolute value at least \(\kappa\), again by \((1)\).  The parameter set
of matrices \(A\) described by the fixed entry, stability-margin, and
separation bounds is compact, and the recursion has finitely many steps.
Thus a finite induction over endpoint gap, using \((11)\) for diagonal
steps and ordinary continuity of addition, multiplication, and division
for edge steps, gives a single \(\delta_0>0\) such that whenever
\(\|\widetilde B-B\|<\delta_0\), both the full and corridor recursions are
defined in a common neighborhood of their population values and all
their displayed denominators have absolute value at least
\(\kappa/2\).  Let \(\mathcal E_n\) be this event with
\(\widetilde B=\widehat B\), together with
\(\widehat M_0\succ0\).  Equation \((10)\) gives
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}P(\mathcal E_n^c)\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{12}
\]

On \(\mathcal E_n\), the full and corridor diagonal roots agree because
both are the unique real odd roots of the same entries \(\widehat B_{ii}\).
Now process an edge \(j\to i\in E_{uv}^{G}\) by increasing endpoint gap.
By
\(\mathrm{lem{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}recursion\mbox{-}closure}\),
every diagonal and strict-edge coordinate in its remainder lies in the
corridor, and every such strict edge has smaller endpoint gap.  Induction
therefore makes the numerator, denominator, and all previously recovered
inputs in the full and corridor updates identical.  Hence
\[
 \widehat A_{ij}^{\mathrm{full}}
 =\widehat A_{ij}^{\mathrm{cor}}
 \quad(j\to i\in E_{uv}^{G}),
 \qquad
 \widehat A_{vv}^{\mathrm{full}}=\widehat A_{vv}^{\mathrm{cor}}.
 \tag{13}
\]
Because \(u\to v\in E_{uv}^{G}\), \((13)\) and the two estimator
definitions imply, simultaneously for every \(z\in\mathcal Z\),
\[
 \widehat h_{uv}(z)
 =\widehat h_{uv}^{\mathrm{cor}}(z)
 =\frac{\widehat A_{vu}^{\mathrm{cor}}z}
 {1-\widehat A_{vv}^{\mathrm{cor}}z}.
 \tag{14}
\]
The computation of \(\widehat Q\) and the subsequent innovation-variance
recovery in the full procedure do not enter the last expression.

Equality \((14)\) holds as an identity of differentiable maps throughout
the common neighborhood defining \(\mathcal E_n\).  Therefore the target
rows of the full and corridor Jacobians are equal there, and those rows
have zero derivatives with respect to non-corridor recursion inputs.
Differentiating the final rational map gives, for either recursion,
\[
 \mathrm dh_{uv}(z)
 =\frac{z\,\mathrm dA_{vu}}{1-A_{vv}z}
  +\frac{A_{vu}z^2\,\mathrm dA_{vv}}{(1-A_{vv}z)^2}.
 \tag{15}
\]
The denominators in \((15)\) are nonzero because
\(|A_{vv}z|\leq1-\gamma<1\).  Since the two procedures use the same
estimated Gaussian lag-moment covariance, equality of their target
Jacobians implies on \(\mathcal E_n\) that
\[
 \widehat\Sigma_h=\widehat\Sigma_{h,\mathrm{cor}},
 \qquad
 \widehat c_{1-\alpha}
 =\widehat c_{1-\alpha}^{\mathrm{cor}}.
 \tag{16}
\]

By \((2)\),
\(\mathrm{thm{:}target\mbox{-}corridor\mbox{-}wald\mbox{-}band}\)
applies to every law in \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\).  Equations
\((12)\), \((14)\), and \((16)\) show that the bounded-Lipschitz distance
between the laws of the full and corridor stacked, scaled transfer
vectors tends to zero uniformly on \(\mathfrak P_{\partial}\).  The same
theorem therefore gives the asserted centered Gaussian limit, with the
Jacobian in \((15)\).

Finally, let \(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{full}}\) and
\(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{cor}}\) be the simultaneous coverage events in the
present theorem and in the corridor theorem, respectively.  By
\((14)\) and \((16)\), they agree on \(\mathcal E_n\).  Hence
\[
\begin{split}
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}
 \left|P(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{full}})-(1-\alpha)\right|
 &\leq
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}
 \left|P(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{cor}})-(1-\alpha)\right|
 +\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}P(\mathcal E_n^c)\\
 &\leq
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{uv,\partial}}
 \left|P(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{cor}})-(1-\alpha)\right|
 +\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_{\partial}}P(\mathcal E_n^c)
 \longrightarrow0,
\end{split}
 \tag{17}
\]
where the second inequality uses \((2)\), the first term tends to zero by
the target-corridor Wald theorem, and the second does so by \((12)\).
Together with \((3)\), this proves both the nonvacuity and every asserted
limit and coverage conclusion.

Fix an arbitrary data-generating law \(P_\star\) in
\(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max})\), write its
fine-grid parameters as \((A_\star,D_\star)\), and denote its stationary
coarse moments by \((M_{0\star},M_{1\star})\).  Define the event
\[
 E_n:=\{(M_{0\star},M_{1\star})\in\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha)\}.
\]
By \(\mathrm{def{:}compact\mbox{-}class}\), \(A_\star\) is lower
triangular and
\(\max_{i\in V}|(A_\star)_{ii}|\leq 1-\gamma\).  Hence
\[
 \det(\lambda I_d-A_\star)
 =\prod_{i\in V}\{\lambda-(A_\star)_{ii}\},
 \qquad
 \rho(A_\star)=\max_{i\in V}|(A_\star)_{ii}|
 \leq 1-\gamma<1.
\]
Thus the stability premise of
\(\mathrm{lem{:}coarse\mbox{-}law\mbox{-}reduction}\) holds.  That lemma
gives \(M_{0\star}\succ0\) and
\[
 M_{1\star}=A_\star^mM_{0\star},
 \qquad
 M_{0\star}=A_\star^mM_{0\star}(A_\star^m)^\top
 +\sum_{r=0}^{m-1}A_\star^rD_\star(A_\star^r)^\top.
\]
Membership in \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}\) also supplies separately the
lower-triangular and graph-support zero restrictions, the bounds
\[
 \max_i|(A_\star)_{ii}|\leq1-\gamma,
 \qquad
 \max_{i,j}|(A_\star)_{ij}|\leq L,
\]
diagonality of \(D_\star\), and
\[
 d_{\min}I_d\preceq D_\star\preceq d_{\max}I_d.
\]
Consequently, on \(E_n\), every constraint in
\(\mathrm{def{:}inverse\mbox{-}region}\) is satisfied by
\((A_\star,D_\star)\), using the existential witnesses
\((M_0,M_1)=(M_{0\star},M_{1\star})\).  Therefore
\[
 E_n\subseteq\{(A_\star,D_\star)\in\mathcal R_n\}.
\]
For every \(z\in\mathbb T\), the stability margin implies
\[
 |1-(A_\star)_{vv}z|
 \geq1-|(A_\star)_{vv}|\,|z|
 \geq\gamma>0,
\]
so \(h_{uv,\star}(z)=(A_\star)_{vu}z/
\{1-(A_\star)_{vv}z\}\) is well defined.  By
\(\mathrm{def{:}transfer\mbox{-}confidence\mbox{-}set}\), membership of
\((A_\star,D_\star)\) in \(\mathcal R_n\) implies
\(h_{uv,\star}\in\mathcal C_n^h\).  Hence
\[
 P_\star\{h_{uv,\star}\in\mathcal C_n^h\}
 \geq P_\star(E_n)
 \geq1-\alpha,
\]
where the last inequality is
\(\mathrm{thm{:}uniform\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}box}\).  Since \(P_\star\)
was arbitrary, this is uniform over the compact class.  The inclusion uses
all stationary moment equations simultaneously and never chooses a matrix
root or divides by a divided difference.

For the final assertion, suppose two compact-class members
\((A^{(1)},D^{(1)})\) and \((A^{(2)},D^{(2)})\) induce the same stationary
coarse moment pair \((M_0,M_1)\), while their queried transfers
\(h_{uv}^{(1)}\) and \(h_{uv}^{(2)}\) are unequal.  On the common event
\[
 E_n^\circ:=\{(M_0,M_1)\in\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha)\},
\]
the coarse-law identities just used and the compact-class restrictions,
applied for each \(k\in\{1,2\}\), give
\[
 (A^{(k)},D^{(k)})\in\mathcal R_n.
\]
The definition of the transfer confidence set therefore yields
\[
 \{h_{uv}^{(1)},h_{uv}^{(2)}\}\subseteq\mathcal C_n^h
 \quad\text{on }E_n^\circ.
\]
Both elements are compatible-class transfers actually attained by models,
not merely limiting values.  This proves the claimed possible
noncontraction and completes the proof.

Fix \(n\geq3\) and a law \(P\) in
\(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}(d,m,G;\gamma,L,d_{\min},d_{\max})\).  Equip
the trajectory space \(\Omega_n=\mathbb R^{(n+1)d}\) with its Borel
\(\sigma\)-field and define
\[
 \widehat K_{\Sigma,n}:\Omega_n\longrightarrow(0,\infty),
 \qquad
 \widehat K_{\Sigma,n}(w):=K_\Sigma.
\]
This map is measurable because, for every Borel set
\(E\subseteq(0,\infty)\), its inverse image is \(\Omega_n\) if
\(K_\Sigma\in E\), and is empty otherwise.

Let \(\Sigma_{n,P}=\operatorname{Cov}_P(W_n)\).  The explicit uniform
coarse spectral-density resolvent bound in
\(\mathrm{thm{:}uniform\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}box}\), under the restrictions
collected in \(\mathrm{def{:}compact\mbox{-}class}\), gives
\[
 0\preceq\Sigma_{n,P}\preceq K_\Sigma I_{(n+1)d},
 \qquad
 \|\Sigma_{n,P}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq K_\Sigma=\widehat K_{\Sigma,n}(W_n)
 \quad P\text{-almost surely}.
\]
Thus the constant measurable envelope dominates the trajectory covariance
uniformly over the compact class.

It is also admissible for the spectral splitting specified by
\(\mathrm{def{:}adaptive\mbox{-}calibration\mbox{-}handle}\).  Indeed, for
a symmetric lag-moment matrix \(H_{\ell ij}\), let
\(H_{\ell ij}=H_{\ell ij}^{+}-H_{\ell ij}^{-}\) be its spectral
positive-negative decomposition, where
\(H_{\ell ij}^{+},H_{\ell ij}^{-}\succeq0\).  For
\(s\in\{+,-\}\), covariance domination and congruence imply
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(H_{\ell ij}^{s}\Sigma_{n,P})
 =\operatorname{tr}\!\left((H_{\ell ij}^{s})^{1/2}
 \Sigma_{n,P}(H_{\ell ij}^{s})^{1/2}\right)
 \leq K_\Sigma\operatorname{tr}(H_{\ell ij}^{s}),
\]
and submultiplicativity gives
\[
 \bigl\|\Sigma_{n,P}^{1/2}H_{\ell ij}^{s}
 \Sigma_{n,P}^{1/2}\bigr\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq \|\Sigma_{n,P}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \|H_{\ell ij}^{s}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq K_\Sigma\|H_{\ell ij}^{s}\|_{\mathrm{op}}.
\]
Thus both spectral parts are controlled by the constant envelope;
recombining them recovers the deterministic two-sided calibration already
certified by \(\mathrm{thm{:}uniform\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}box}\).

Define, for every realized trajectory,
\[
 \widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^M(\alpha):=\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha),
 \qquad
 \widetilde{\mathcal R}_n:=\mathcal R_n,
 \qquad
 \widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^h:=\mathcal C_n^h.
\]
For each \((\ell,i,j)\in\{0,1\}\times V\times V\), the corresponding
coordinate interval is therefore exactly
\[
 \operatorname{Out}_N\!\left((\widehat M_\ell)_{ij},
 2K_\Sigma\left\{
 \sqrt{\frac{\log(4d^2/\alpha)}{n}}
 +\frac{\log(4d^2/\alpha)}{n}\right\}\right),
\]
the deterministic-\(K_\Sigma\) interval of
\(\mathrm{def{:}moment\mbox{-}box}\).  Thus every fallback coordinate
width equals, and hence is no larger than, its deterministic counterpart at
every sample point.  In particular,
\[
 P\!\left\{\text{all fallback coordinate widths are no larger than their
 deterministic-\(K_\Sigma\) counterparts}\right\}=1.
\]
Moreover, equality of the moment regions and
\(\mathrm{thm{:}uniform\mbox{-}moment\mbox{-}box}\) yield
\[
 \inf_{P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}}
 P\{(M_0,M_1)\in\widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^M(\alpha)\}
 =
 \inf_{P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{cmp}}}
 P\{(M_0,M_1)\in\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha)\}
 \geq1-\alpha.
\]
Every endpoint is rational by the defining property of
\(\operatorname{Out}_N\).  Finally,
\(\widetilde{\mathcal R}_n=\mathcal R_n\) leaves all polynomial equalities
and inequalities in \(\mathrm{def{:}inverse\mbox{-}region}\) unchanged,
and \(\widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^h=\mathcal C_n^h\) leaves the transfer
projection unchanged.  Hence the rational encoding and exact branch-free
semialgebraic inverse are preserved.  By
\(\mathrm{thm{:}global\mbox{-}honest\mbox{-}inversion}\), the same
equalities also preserve finite-sample transfer coverage.  Since every
width comparison is an equality, no strict adaptive improvement is claimed.

Apply \(\mathrm{thm{:}adaptive\mbox{-}calibration\mbox{-}fallback}\) for
each \(n\geq3\).  It supplies the measurable constant envelope
\(\widehat K_{\Sigma,n}\equiv K_\Sigma\) and proves, sample by sample,
\[
 \widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^M(\alpha)=\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha),
 \qquad
 \widetilde{\mathcal R}_n=\mathcal R_n,
 \qquad
 \widetilde{\mathcal C}_n^h=\mathcal C_n^h.
\]
The first equality makes every coordinate interval exactly as wide as its
deterministic-\(K_\Sigma\) counterpart.  Therefore the coordinatewise
no-wider event is the whole trajectory sample space and has probability one
under every compact-class law for every \(n\).  In particular, for each
interior regular law belonging to that class, this probability sequence is
identically one and hence converges to one.  The same fallback theorem gives
uniform finite-sample coverage at least \(1-\alpha\), rational outward
rounding, and preservation of the exact branch-free semialgebraic inverse.
Because this construction gives equality of widths, it proves no strict
adaptive improvement.

theorem.statement:
There exists a measurable choice within \(\mathrm{CalHandle}\) such that,
for every \(n\geq3\), its moment region has finite-sample coverage at least
\(1-\alpha\) uniformly over the compact class, its endpoints are rationally
outward rounded by \(\operatorname{Out}_N\), and its exact branch-free
semialgebraic inverse through \(\mathcal R_n\) is preserved.  For every
interior regular law in that class, the probability that all coordinate
intervals are no wider than the deterministic-\(K_\Sigma\) intervals of
\(\mathcal C_n^M(\alpha)\) tends to one.  Thus the adaptive-calibration
question has an affirmative answer in its literal weak \emph{no wider}
sense, but this existential conclusion does not require a strict width
improvement.
theorem.proof_tex:
The claim is the direct existential consequence of
\(\mathrm{thm{:}adaptive\mbox{-}calibration\mbox{-}literal\mbox{-}answer}\).
That theorem supplies a constant envelope and the three region
equalities for every \(n\geq3\), proves the probability-one coordinatewise
width equality, and establishes uniform finite-sample coverage, rational
outward rounding, and preservation of exact branch-free inversion.  Since a
probability identically equal to one converges to one, all clauses in the
stated answer follow.  Its equality-of-widths qualification also gives the
final limitation.

proofs.proof_tex:
Formally specialize Definitions~\(\texttt{def:compatible-fiber}\) and \(\texttt{def:certificate}\) to \(m=1\). Let \((A,D)\in\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\). The first compatibility equation in Definition~\(\texttt{def:compatible-fiber}\) gives
\[
B=A^1=A.
\]
The second compatibility equation in that definition, together with \(A^0=I_d\), gives
\[
Q=\sum_{r=0}^{1-1}A^rD(A^r)^\top
  =A^0D(A^0)^\top
  =D.
\]
Thus every member of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\) equals \((B,Q)\), and the fiber has at most one member.

Conversely, substitute \((A,D)=(B,Q)\) into Definition~\(\texttt{def:compatible-fiber}\). The two coarse equations hold identically because \(B^1=B\) and
\[
\sum_{r=0}^{0}B^rQ(B^r)^\top=B^0Q(B^0)^\top=Q.
\]
The remaining conditions in that definition hold if and only if
\[
B_{ij}=0\quad(i<j),
\qquad
B_{ij}=0\quad(i>j\ \text{and}\ j\to i\notin G),
\]
\[
\max_i|B_{ii}|<1,
\qquad
Q_{ij}=0\quad(i\ne j),
\qquad
Q\succ0.
\]
These are exactly the fine-grid compatibility constraints obtained by the stated formal specialization. Therefore
\[
\mathcal S(B,Q;G)=
\begin{cases}
\{(B,Q)\},&\text{if all of the displayed compatibility constraints hold},\\
\varnothing,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

It remains to verify the asserted algorithmic output. Under \(m=1\), each enumerated diagonal-root equation is
\[
a_{ii}^{1}=B_{ii},
\]
and hence has the unique real solution \(a_{ii}=B_{ii}\). The declared divided-difference polynomial satisfies
\[
C_1(x,y)=\sum_{r=0}^{0}x^r y^{0-r}=1.
\]
Moreover, a nondecreasing walk of length one has at most one strict increase, whereas the declared remainder contains only monomials indexed by walks with at least two strict increases. Hence every such remainder at this specialization is zero. The lower-triangular root identity processed by the graph recursion consequently reduces, at each allowed off-diagonal coordinate, to
\[
B_{ij}=A_{ij}C_1(A_{ii},A_{jj})+0=A_{ij}.
\]
Thus no divided-difference coefficient is singular, and the recursive enumeration has the unique transition candidate \(A=B\). The coarse covariance equation then has the unique innovation candidate \(D=Q\). By Definition~\(\texttt{def:certificate}\), its exact compatibility test rejects this candidate exactly when it fails one of the defining constraints of \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)\). The fiber characterization above therefore implies that the certificate returns incompatibility precisely when \(\mathcal S(B,Q;G)=\varnothing\), and otherwise accepts the unique compatible pair \((B,Q)\).

In the latter case, two compatible copies in the certificate's transfer-inequality test must both equal \((B,Q)\), so no two transfer-distinct witnesses exist. The certificate therefore returns the common transfer, which by the declared definition of \(h_{uv}\) is
\[
h_{uv}(z)=\frac{A_{vu}z}{1-A_{vv}z}
          =\frac{B_{vu}z}{1-B_{vv}z}.
\]
Compatibility gives \(|B_{vv}|<1\). Since \(z\in\mathbb T\) entails \(|z|=1\),
\[
|B_{vv}z|=|B_{vv}|<1,
\]
and therefore \(1-B_{vv}z\ne0\). The returned rational function is consequently well defined on \(\mathbb T\); because \(A=B\), it is exactly the unaliased direct fine-grid process transfer. This proves the proposition.
